title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
claim: A small aligned teacher is trained separately, then its frozen internal representation structure is distilled into a student while the student keeps its original task objective.
layout: 2 panels side by side, left-to-right data flow; (a) independent pre-training, (b) distillation with dashed layer selection boxes, loss arrows beneath/beside networks
description: Two framed panels. Panel (a), "Independent model pre-training", shows two separate flows. At the top, a cylinder labeled D_teacher holding four small sample images feeds an arrow into a small three-layer teacher network. Loss arrows point to L_align, a black forward arrow and a red backward arrow. At the bottom, a larger cylinder D_student with a 3x3 image grid feeds a four-layer student network, with L_task on the right. Panel (b), "Layer selection + representation-structure distillation", repeats both networks. The teacher is frozen, marked by a blue snowflake. The student is the same four-layer network. Dashed boxes mark one selected layer in each network. Each selected layer produces a colorful similarity matrix heatmap. A red arrow labeled L_rep links the two heatmaps and runs back to the student. L_task stays on the student. Light blue nodes mark the teacher and light pink nodes mark the student.
caption: Overview of BIRD: (a) First, a student model is pre-trained using generic optimization approaches on its target training set, Dstudent. A teacher model is independently trained to develop aligned behavior (e.g., robustness) on dataset Dteacher (optimizing an alignment objective, Lalign). (b) Next, the student model is fine-tuned on its original dataset to maintain task performance while learning latent representations with similar structure to that of the (frozen) teacher in selected layers.
abstract: Human-aligned deep learning models exhibit behaviors consistent with human values, such as robustness, fairness, and honesty. Transferring these behavioral properties to models trained on different tasks or data distributions remains challenging: aligned behavior is easily forgotten during fine-tuning, and collecting task-specific data that preserves this behavior can be prohibitively costly. We introduce BIRD (Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation), a flexible framework for transferring aligned behavior by matching the internal representation structure of a student model to that of a teacher. Applied to out-of-distribution robustness in image classification, BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the next strongest baseline. It remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is $25 \times$ smaller than the student. In a large-scale study of over 400 teacher-student pairs, we show that three interpretable and computable properties of the teacher's representations (i.e., task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success. These insights offer practical guidance for teacher selection and design. BIRD turns small, well-aligned models into scalable alignment seeds, removing a key bottleneck in deploying safe AI systems in the wild.
